name: Watching-eye effect
statement: A picture of eyes is said to make people behave better when nobody is really watching, from paying for coffee to dropping less litter.
meaning: The claim has two parts. The first is that humans carry machinery for detecting observation and adjusting conduct to protect a reputation. The second is that the machinery is crude enough to fire on a photograph. Nothing about a printed pair of eyes can carry information to anyone, so a person who gives more, litters less or steals less in front of one is responding to a cue that cannot possibly cost or reward them. That is what makes the finding interesting and what makes it fragile. The effect is not the ordinary observation effect, which is large and uncontested: people do behave differently when a real person can see them. The watching-eye claim is that an image with no informational content produces a measurable share of the same response.

origin.who: Kevin J. Haley and Daniel M. T. Fessler
origin.note: Their dictator-game paper, "Nobody's watching?", put stylised eyespots on a computer desktop and reported more giving. The demonstration that made the idea famous came a year later, when Bateson, Nettle and Roberts ran the honesty box in a Newcastle coffee room.

evidence: Bateson, Nettle and Roberts hung a notice above an honesty box in the coffee room of the Division of Psychology at Newcastle University. Its 150 by 35 millimetre banner alternated each week between a pair of eyes and an image of flowers, over ten weeks. Tea, coffee and milk cost 30, 50 and 10 pence, and 48 people used the facility, 25 women and 23 men. Milk consumption served as the index of how much was drunk. People paid 2.76 times as much per litre of milk in the eyes weeks, 0.417 pounds plus or minus 0.081 against 0.151 plus or minus 0.030. A general linear model on log-transformed data explained 63.8 percent of the variance, with a main effect of image type, F(1,7) = 11.551, p = 0.011, and no effect of week, F(1,7) = 0.074, p = 0.794. The unit of analysis was the week, so the significant result rests on ten numbers. Haley and Fessler's earlier dictator game used five conditions, combining eyespots on the desktop with sound-deadening earmuffs meant to remove auditory cues of other people. Northover and colleagues, who obtained the data, place that study at 124 participants and score it as Hedges' g = 0.30, 95% confidence interval -0.06 to 0.67 for the amount given, and a log odds ratio of 1.21, 95% CI 0.42 to 2.01, for the proportion who gave anything. The second of those two numbers, not the first, is the finding the paper is remembered for.

replication.headline: Pooled across 26 experiments, eye images moved the amount people gave by Hedges' g = 0.03; pooled across 15 experiments on antisocial behaviour, they cut it by about a third.
replication.detail: Northover, Pedersen, Cohen and Andrews ran two meta-analyses on generosity in 2017. The first covered the mean amount given: 26 experiments, 2,732 participants, 18 papers of which one was unpublished, and 2 theses. The random-effects estimate was Hedges' g = 0.03, SE 0.05, 95% CI -0.08 to 0.13, with Q(25) = 40.81, p = .02. The second covered whether a person gave anything at all, the version of the claim Nettle and colleagues had argued for: 27 experiments, 19,512 participants, log odds ratio 0.16, SE 0.10, which is an odds ratio of 1.17, interval -0.04 to 0.35 on the log scale, Q(26) = 34.98, p = .11. A companion paper the same year pooled six experiments on moral judgement. The wallet vignette gave a mean difference of -0.05, SE 0.18, 95% CI -0.40 to 0.30 on a nine-point scale across 1,350 participants; the resume vignette gave -0.21, SE 0.11, 95% CI -0.43 to -0.00003 across 1,346, which its own authors call barely significant. Against that sits Dear, Dutton and Fox, who in 2019 pooled 15 experiments from 13 papers on antisocial behaviour rather than generosity. Setting aside three field studies, their random-effects estimate was a log odds ratio of -0.45, SE 0.18, 95% CI -0.81 to -0.09, p = .01, an odds ratio of 0.64. Adding the three back, the random-effects estimate held at -0.43, SE 0.17, 95% CI -0.76 to -0.11, but the fixed-effects estimate fell to -0.13, SE 0.05, 95% CI -0.23 to -0.03, an odds ratio of 0.88 and a reduction nearer 12 percent. Two broader pools land in between. Bradley, Lawrence and Ferguson meta-analysed observability and prosociality across 117 papers, 134 study-level effects and 788,164 people, finding r = 0.141, 95% CI 0.106 to 0.175 overall. Their perceived-observability subgroup, the one containing eye images, gave r = 0.100, 95% CI 0.050 to 0.149, k = 49, against r = 0.352, 95% CI 0.225 to 0.478, k = 12, for a live passive observer. Wang and colleagues pooled 216 effect sizes from 91 articles in 2023 and report a log odds ratio of 0.231 and Hedges' g = 0.117.

study.cite: Northover, S. B., Pedersen, W. C., Cohen, A. B., & Andrews, P. W. (2017). Artificial surveillance cues do not increase generosity: two meta-analyses. Evolution and Human Behavior, 38(1), 144-153.

limits: The honesty box has not survived close inspection. Carbon and Hesslinger reran Bateson's own analysis and found the general linear model rested on unequal error variances, Bartlett's test chi-squared = 121.8, p < .0001. Repeating it uncorrected reproduced the published result, F(1,7) = 11.82, p = .011, partial eta squared 0.628. Correcting for the violated assumption gave F(2,7) = 4.56, p = .054. Their own laboratory experiment with 138 volunteers found no effect of the social cue on any of four socially relevant scenarios, F(1,133) < 1, p = .5618. The moderators offered to rescue the effect have their own record. Sparks and Barclay proposed that eyes work only briefly, and their 188-participant dictator game found more giving under sudden eyespots than under constant ones, t(131) = 3.04, p = 0.003, though the contrast against no eyes reached only t(122) = 1.67, p = 0.049. Eight years later Sparks and Barclay were co-authors on a preregistered attempt with 355 students that found nothing: means of 3.80 dollars watched by peers, 4.31 with eyes and 3.97 in control, F(2,353) = 1.02, p = .360, partial eta squared .006. Oda argues the opposite way, that the null meta-analyses pooled classroom surveys and online labour markets with controlled laboratory sessions, and so ignored the one variable field studies keep finding matters, how many real people are nearby. He offers no reanalysis. Dear and colleagues' own set is small and uneven: of 15 experiments, one corruption experiment carries a log odds ratio of -1.78 and two run the wrong way, engine idling at 0.63 and a national dog-fouling campaign at 0.10. Heterogeneity in the wider literature is extreme; Bradley and colleagues report I-squared of 99.24.
misreadings: The 2.76 figure is the most quoted number in this literature and the least transferable. It is one coffee room, one department, ten weekly observations, and money per litre of milk rather than per person. No individual decision was recorded, so nothing in it says what a given person did. The second error is treating the two meta-analytic camps as if they answered the same question. Northover and colleagues pooled generosity, and found nothing. Dear, Dutton and Fox pooled littering, dishonesty, corruption and theft, and found a reduction. Neither result is evidence about the other, and Dear's team says as much in setting up their review. The third error involves Sparks and Barclay's 2013 paper, widely cited as a meta-analysis confirming the effect at short exposures. It pooled no effect sizes. It classified 25 experiments by whether any effect was reported and by exposure length, then ran Fisher's exact tests on the resulting table: 15 of 16 short-exposure studies reported an effect, none of 5 prolonged-exposure studies did, p < 0.005. A vote count of published outcomes is the design most exposed to whatever kept the null results out of print. Fourth, Nettle and colleagues' formulation, that eyes change whether you give rather than how much, is often cited as the surviving version of the effect. Northover's second meta-analysis tested exactly that formulation on 19,512 people and its interval crossed zero. Fifth, none of this touches the ordinary observation effect. Bradley and colleagues put a live passive observer at r = 0.352 against r = 0.100 for a cue that only implies observation, and the gap between those two numbers is the whole subject.
